cases.title: Noor Ouarzazate Solar Complex: Lost Pasture and Water
cases.place: Ghassate commune, north of Ouarzazate, Morocco
cases.point: Noor Ouarzazate solar site, north of Ouarzazate (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD/IDA)
lenders.role: US$519 million for the complex (Equal Times, 2016).

lenders.name: KfW (Germany)
lenders.role: €654 million, about US$690 million (Equal Times, 2016).

lenders.name: African Development Bank
lenders.role: Support for the complex, amount not given (Equal Times, 2016).

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: Support for the complex, amount not given (Equal Times, 2016).

lenders.name: European Commission
lenders.role: Support for the complex, amount not given (Equal Times, 2016).

cases.conditions: The lenders financed a solar complex on about 3,000 hectares of collective land, which Morocco's solar agency MASEN bought in 2010. The African Development Bank's own summary describes the land as grazing land with very little pasture, says herders would lose passage through the site, and proposes grazing between the panels as compensation (AfDB, 2011).

companies.name: ACWA Power
companies.role: Saudi company leading the consortium that builds the plants and sells power to MASEN for 25 years (MERIP, 2021)

companies.name: MASEN (Moroccan Agency for Solar Energy)
companies.role: Bought the land and runs the complex

cases.community: About 8,000 villagers lost access to collective pasture in 2010 (Zakia Salime, MERIP, 2021; also Asmaa Elgamal, Harvard Weatherhead Center, 2024); neither gives the origin of the figure. Sarah Ryser's 2015 to 2018 fieldwork, published in a peer-reviewed journal, records herders describing closed paths and lost access to the plateau, without a count. The land was sold at about 1 dirham per square metre, 32 million dirhams in total (Equal Times, 2016); MERIP gives 15 US cents per square metre and over $3.5 million. Some Ghassate residents thought the price too low and felt poorly consulted (World Resources Institute, 2021). A resident told MERIP that the shared electricity bill for pumping drinking water nears $500 a month, and MERIP's author writes that water tables are falling. Noor draws an estimated 2.5 to 3 million cubic metres a year from a reservoir nearby communities also use (WRI). MASEN promised 2,000 to 3,000 construction jobs; the finished site will be run by no more than 40 engineers and technicians (MERIP).
cases.outcome: The sale money went to a rural affairs account for a social development plan of about 30.5 million dirhams (WRI). MASEN also funds roads, canal repair and school transport (MERIP). Protests took place during construction (Germanwatch adviser, via Equal Times).

sources.title: Life in the Vicinity of Morocco's Noor Solar Energy Project
sources.publisher: Middle East Research and Information Project

sources.title: Is the world's largest solar project a "green megawatt" or a "green grab"?
Morocco: Ensuring a Large-scale Renewable Installation Benefits Local Communities
The Anti-Politics Machine of Green Energy Development: The Moroccan Solar Project in Ouarzazate
Commodifying the Desert: Colonial Formulas and Ancestral Lands in Morocco's Renewable Energy Sector
Ouarzazate solar power station: ESIA executive summary
sources.publisher: African Development Bank, via Land Matrix

cases.confidence_note: Timing: the community approved the sale on 14 January 2010 and it was final on 18 October 2010 (AfDB), before the AfDB's 2011 review, so the lenders came after the sale and financed the fenced site that kept the land closed. WRI says the site was not populated, the AfDB says no one had to move, and WRI says residents overwhelmingly supported the project. One estimate puts Noor I's water use below 1% of the reservoir. The 8,000 figure has no stated origin. The link between the plant and falling water tables is unproven.

lvwhy.land: Collective pasture was sold for the site.

cases.title: Cairo Metro Line 3: Zamalek Building Evacuated and Resettlement Complaints
cases.point: Zamalek, near Brazil Street, where the neighbouring Bahrain Embassy stands; a 12-storey building beside it was evacuated in July 2020 (approximate)

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: Funds 15% of the project; agreed in 2012 to accept complaints and pass them to the National Authority for Tunnels; suspended funding for a time in 2013 (Mada Masr, 2016).

cases.conditions: EIB financing for Phase 3 of Line 3. Its 2013 report flagged soil and building condition and recommended building-by-building foundation checks, without requiring a route change (Mada Masr, 2016).
cases.community: In July 2020 a 12-storey Zamalek building near the works was evacuated after reports of cracks and tilting; first inspections found sinkholes under the garage and near the entrance, and the Bahrain Embassy next door was also damaged (Scoop Empire; Daily News Egypt; Egypt Today). Residents got EGP 30,000 each for temporary housing; one said the sum, 1,000 pounds a day for a month, was not enough for a family, and that belongings were left behind (Scoop Empire). Separately, complainants told the EIB Complaints Mechanism that resettlement compensation was inadequate; one, temporarily resettled, reported slow and inadequate payment and asked for a report on their building's condition.
cases.outcome: Dredging stopped for a week, and the contractor was to pay for repairs (Egypt Today). The EIB office recorded non-compliance in case SG/E/2017/53, closed in September 2022 (Accountability Console); it closed SG/E/2020/22 in March 2023 and SG/E/2017/10 in December 2024. A lawsuit by residents was before the courts in 2016 (Mada Masr).

cases.confidence_note: Officials gave different accounts. The Tunnels Authority called it slight subsidence near an old building and denied that underground works caused it, and the minister said the building was not leaning and had no cracks; yet Egypt Today and Daily News Egypt reported the damage as caused by the works, and the contractor was to pay. Details of the compensation complaints are confidential, and no sum or number of households is public.

lvwhy.project: EIB co-financed the metro works reported to have damaged the building.

cases.title: Maritsa East Mines: Beli Bryag Village
cases.place: Beli Bryag, Maritsa East coal basin, Bulgaria
cases.point: Beli Bryag village, in the centre of the Maritsa East coalfield (coordinates from the mine's resettlement plan)

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
lenders.role: Grant of €15.15 million through the Kozloduy decommissioning fund it manages, approved 2013 (EBRD); Bankwatch says it paid half of a €25.8 million excavator upgrade; €80 million in a 2016 Bulgarian Energy Holding bond and €100 million in a 2018 one (EBRD; Bankwatch, 2021).

cases.conditions: The bond and loan contracts carried environmental and social conditions, but barred EBRD money only from coal and nuclear power plants, not coal mines (Bankwatch). The mine's Resettlement Action Plan follows EBRD Performance Requirement 5 on land and displacement.
cases.community: The mine's own Resettlement Action Plan (2018) says residents will be physically and economically displaced and all structures demolished. It counted 148 registered residents in 69 households in 2016, and 116 people in 49 households living there, 65 of them classed as vulnerable. Intensive resettlement began in 2009, and about 75% of the land was acquired by then. The national census recorded 143 people in 2011 and 56 in 2021. Six residents told the EBRD's accountability office that the expansion cost the community land and income (EBRD). Bankwatch reports that the last residents live with constant vibration, noise and dust, interrupted water and electricity, and no shops or public transport. The deadline for voluntary sale was December 2019, with expropriation after that (RAP; Bankwatch). In 2024 a resident, Petar Tanev, sued the Energy Ministry for requiring him to leave (BTA).
cases.outcome: Mediation under a 2017 complaint closed in August 2020 with no agreement. A second request was registered in 2021; the office finished a compliance assessment in April 2022, and the case is listed at the compliance review stage with no findings on its page.

sources.title: Maritsa East Mines, case 2021/03
At Bulgarian coal mine, a climate and human rights crisis unfolds
Man Sues Energy Ministry for Forcing Him to Move Out for Coal Mines' Expansion
Resettlement Action Plan, Beli Bryag
Beli Brjag population
sources.publisher: City Population, from Bulgaria's National Statistical Institute

cases.confidence_note: Displacement is confirmed by the mine's own plan. Daily living conditions come from Bankwatch, which supports the complainants; the EBRD office has published no findings on its case page. Resettlement began in 2009, before the EBRD's first money here (2013 grant), and continued under it. Bankwatch says the company argued that Bulgarian law conflicts with EBRD standards.

lvwhy.project: EBRD grant paid for mine excavators.
lvwhy.finance: EBRD bonds freed cash that reached the mine.
lvwhy.land: Villagers lost land to the mine's expansion.

cases.title: Adriatic Metals' Vareš Mine: Forest and Streams
cases.place: Rupice mine, Vareš, and Trstionica forest, Kakanj, Bosnia and Herzegovina
cases.point: Rupice underground mine, about 8.7 km west of Vareš (approximate)

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
lenders.role: Equity of GBP 6.2 million (€6.84 million) in Adriatic Metals PLC, approved 6 October 2020, first 2.6% of shares and later about 1.9%. EBRD says the money paid for studies, not mine building (IPAM, 2023).

cases.conditions: EBRD money supported engineering and economic studies, including the Bankable Feasibility Study, and pre-development costs. EBRD says it monitors the mine's development as part of its shareholding and does not finance it.

companies.name: Adriatic Metals PLC
companies.role: Owner of the zinc, lead and barytes mine

cases.community: 103 residents of the Trstionica and Boriva area in Kakanj complained of forest cutting, water pollution, noise, vibration and landslides, and said the rivers once served about 40,000 people (IPAM). The company admitted that its first civil works raised sediment and clouded water, and that monitoring showed some loss of aquatic life during construction, for which it has a restoration plan for the Vruci stream (IPAM, 2023). Bankwatch found on a November 2022 visit that an access road not in the environmental studies had been built on a widened forest path, narrowing a stream. In July 2023 federal inspectors announced violations at a mine site: a landfill with no lining or fence, and no concrete channels or sedimentation tank (Bankwatch).
cases.suppression: The 103 requesters kept their names confidential, citing fear of retaliation (IPAM).
cases.outcome: IPAM was asked for a compliance review only. It completed a compliance assessment in August 2024, and the case is listed as open at the review stage. Inspectors gave the company a deadline to comply.

sources.title: Assessment Report, DFF Adriatic Metals, case 2022/02
DFF Adriatic Metals, case 2022/02
Adriatic Metals: ruthless mining; how can EBRD help improve its clients' practices?

cases.confidence_note: The company says its water tests show the project is not polluting rivers, that permits were in place, and that rock waste was removed; requesters say the waste was not removed and the water is no longer drinkable. A subcontractor agreed to remove a temporary concrete plant. EBRD bought its shares in October 2020, before construction began in 2021, and held them when the harm occurred, but did not finance construction. IPAM records the pollution claims as allegations and has not published findings on its case page.
cases.ecosystem: Bankwatch reports the Vrući potok stream habitat seriously damaged and muddy in November 2022. The company acknowledges some aquatic biodiversity loss during construction.

lvwhy.project: The mine's early works damaged a stream.
lvwhy.finance: EBRD bought shares in the mine owner.

cases.title: Georgia East–West Highway: Rikoti Pass Landslides and Khevi Homes
cases.point: Rikoti Pass on the E-60 highway; the Chumateleti-Khevi section runs about 9 to 12 km from the Rikoti tunnel to Khevi (approximate)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Khevi–Ubisa (F2) and Shorapani–Argveta (F4) sections (Bankwatch, 2024). Shorapani–Argveta is Loan 3861 in a project costing $367.4 million (ADB).

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: Chumateleti–Khevi (F1) and Ubisa–Shorapani (F3) sections (Bankwatch, 2024).

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD/IDA)
lenders.role: Chumateleti–Khevi (F1) section (Bankwatch, 2024).

cases.conditions: The lenders financed sections of the E-60 highway built on steep slopes and through tunnels, for a total of about GEL 3 billion (Bankwatch, 2024).
cases.community: Landslides in April and May 2023 led to 23 new complaints on the Chumateleti-Khevi section, three of them asking for resettlement (World Bank report, via Bankwatch); at least one family was still waiting for a decision in February 2024. Residents allege cracked homes from blasting and describe nights of noise from tunnelling under their houses. Waste deposits narrowed the Rikotula river beside the Khevi school, which about 150 children attend (Bankwatch). A family told the EIB office of house damage on the Ubisa-Shorapani section (EIB). At Zestafoni, two residents told ADB of split walls, lost road access, damaged utility lines and a well that fell about 3 metres; an independent engineer did not attribute the structural damage to the highway (ADB).
cases.outcome: ADB's facilitator closed the Zestafoni complaint without agreement after the Roads Department said in October 2025 that it could not engage further. The EIB case was under compliance review in 2026 after dispute resolution failed. The Roads Department reports 78 meetings in 2023; residents say these changed little.

sources.title: The promise and perils of Georgia's East–West Highway project
SPF 2024/25: Final Report, East–West Highway (Shorapani–Argveta)
E-60 Ubisa–Shorapani Section F3, SG/E/2025/10

E60 Chumateleti-Khevi Section F1

cases.confidence_note: An independent engineer for ADB found one Zestafoni house unchanged from its 2021 survey and the other run down from lack of maintenance, with no structural damage attributable to the highway. The Roads Department says the well issue cannot be tied to construction. Whether the road caused the damage in the EIB case is not settled. Experts cited by Bankwatch say landslides increased after building began on the pass; no official finding says so. The World Bank did not respond to Business & Human Rights Resource Centre.

lvwhy.project: Banks financed sections of the highway where damage is reported.

cases.title: Amulsar Gold Mine: Gndevaz and Jermuk
cases.point: Gndevaz village, next to the Amulsar mine (approximate)

lenders.name: IFC
lenders.role: Invested $16.4 million in the developer, Lydian, from 2007 and sold all its shares in May 2017, CAO reports. The sale became public in September 2017 (Accountability Console; Lydian). A campaign summary dates IFC's support to 2021 (BHRRC), which CAO's report contradicts.

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
lenders.role: Investor in Lydian, with a further CAD 11.4 million approved in July 2016 for environmental and social measures. Its stake ended with a 2020 restructuring, which EBRD said was not a voluntary exit (Accountability Console). A campaign summary dates its backing to 2017 (BHRRC).

cases.conditions: Equity stakes in the mine's developer during exploration and construction.

companies.name: Lydian International
companies.role: Parent of the mine developer Lydian Armenia (earlier Geoteam)

cases.community: In 2014, while IFC was an investor, Gndevaz villagers told its complaint office that produce was hard to sell and that residents who did not want to leave were being forced to sell land (CAO complaint). After construction began in 2017, while EBRD was an investor, Gndevaz residents reported dark, muddy water in drinking and irrigation pipes and hundreds of dead fish on farms, and said livestock refused grass and water. In a survey of households in Gndevaz, Kechout and Jermuk, 85.7% of respondents reported illnesses since construction began (Accountability Console). CAO found IFC's assessment of effects on Gndevaz and on Jermuk's tourism did not meet requirements, while finding IFC compliant on groundwater risk (CAO; Accountability Console).
cases.suppression: Lydian filed about 20 defamation lawsuits against critics between 2018 and 2020 (Accountability Console). FIDH, Bankwatch and partners refer to dozens of such suits (BHRRC, 2022).
cases.outcome: From June 2018, residents blockaded all four main roads to the mine for over two years. CAO closed its cases in October 2018 without remedy because IFC no longer had an investment. An EBRD compliance review began in November 2020 and was still going in May 2023 (Accountability Console).

sources.title: Water is our gold: lessons from a community struggle in Armenia
Complaint to the CAO from the villagers of Gndevaz
Armenia: report calls on revoking license for exploitation of gold mine in Amulsar
Compliance monitoring report: Lydian International, complaints 01 and 02
Armenia: Lydian Intl3-02/Gndevaz
Lydian International's response to article about IFC's divestment

cases.confidence_note: The pollution and health figures come from residents and a survey; no official measurement was seen. CAO found failures to assess impacts, not proof of the harm. IFC left in May 2017, about when construction began, so its overlap is with the 2014 land claims; EBRD's overlaps with the later pollution claims. Lydian replied to news of IFC's exit by pointing to economic growth, not to the health claims.

lvwhy.project: Construction of the mine is the reported source of pollution.
lvwhy.finance: IFC and EBRD held shares in the developer.

cases.title: Shah Deniz 2 and the Sangachal Terminal: Village Health Complaints
cases.point: Sangachal village, beside BP's gas terminal (approximate)

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
lenders.role: A $500 million loan to Lukoil, an investor in Shah Deniz 2, in place by the 2017 complaint and repaid in October 2021 (OCCRP, 2022).

cases.conditions: A 2017 complaint argued that the board approved the investment three months before the independent audit was finished; OCCRP says the complaint office backed much of that account.

companies.name: BP
companies.role: Operator of the Sangachal terminal and client

cases.community: Nine villagers told Crude Accountability in 2021 of breathing and heart problems and skin rashes they link to flaring at the terminal. They say flaring sometimes shakes homes hard enough to break objects, that yellow dust stains washing, and that plants and animals have been poisoned. None had received compensation (OCCRP, 2022). Satellite data show flaring rose after 2018. A 2019 air sample from a nearby village showed raised sulphur dioxide, but its source could not be confirmed. Requesters to the EBRD also alleged poor consultation and compensation, harm to the village's farming and property damage from a 2016 pipeline explosion.
cases.outcome: The EBRD office found non-compliance and published its report on 5 April 2019; a Management Action Plan followed in May 2019. Monitoring closed in May 2023. EBRD declined to comment to OCCRP on villagers' health accounts.

sources.title: The People Paying the Price of Shah Deniz 2's Success
Lukoil Shah Deniz Stage II, case 2017/07
Lukoil Shah Deniz Stage II

cases.confidence_note: The harm is villagers' testimony, not a measurement. BP says monitoring from 2018 to 2021 found no emissions above legal limits and recorded no environmental grievances from these communities. SOCAR says it does not operate Sangachal. Other pollution sources exist, including a power plant running since 2008. The EBRD office's non-compliance finding is recorded, but its case page describes the harm only as allegations. EBRD's loan went to a minority investor in the gas field, not to the terminal. Villagers' names were changed.

lvwhy.project: The gas field's output runs through the terminal the village sits beside.
lvwhy.finance: EBRD lent to an investor in the field.

cases.title: Trans Adriatic Pipeline in Albania: Farmers' Land and Trees
cases.place: Pipeline route through Korçë, Berat and Fier regions, Albania
cases.point: Poshnje, Berat region, one of the villages on the route (approximate; the route runs about 200 km)

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: €700 million direct loan with an EU guarantee (EIB, 2019).

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
lenders.role: €500 million A loan and €500 million B loan from commercial banks (EIB, 2019).

lenders.name: Export credit agencies (bpifrance, Euler Hermes, SACE)
lenders.role: €450 million, €280 million and €700 million in cover (EIB, 2019).

lenders.name: Commercial banks
lenders.role: €635 million without agency cover; 17 banks in all (EIB, 2019).

cases.conditions: €3.9 billion project financing closed in December 2018. Costs before that were paid by the shareholders (EIB, 2019).

companies.name: Trans Adriatic Pipeline AG
companies.role: Pipeline company, owned by BP, SOCAR and Snam (20% each), Fluxys (19%), Enagás (16%) and Axpo (5%)

cases.community: About 80 Albanian communities, most reliant on farming, were affected (Balkan Insight, 2016). In July 2016 Bankwatch interviewed people in 32 villages. One Fushë-Peshtan farmer was losing 230 olive trees aged 18 and two Otllek brothers and their father 100 olive trees about 80 years old. Land at Munushtir was paid as category III, €0.25 per square metre, though farmers said it fit category I, €0.39. One owner was offered 161,000 and then 364,000 lek and then served an expropriation notice for 230,000 lek. At Seman, machinery cracked a house and damaged water pipes, and the owner said at least five other houses had cracks. A May 2017 mission with the Albanian Helsinki Committee reported insufficient compensation, a lack of legal help and some intimidation (Bankwatch).
cases.suppression: Farmers at Zemblak and Uznove said they were told to sign or face problems with the state or expropriation (Bankwatch, 2016).
cases.outcome: Four families complained to the EIB in 2016 (Balkan Insight). The EIB office found the bank had not finished its checks or decided to finance, passed one complaint to its staff, and they replied that TAP AG held responsibility for land. The government set a total package of €2,334,515 in September 2016.

sources.title: "We have no other option": Albanian communities face unjust resettlement process
No other option: TAP fact-finding mission, Albania

Albanians Dispute New Pipeline Compensation Rates
SG/E/2016/16/PR Trans Adriatic Pipeline
TAP completes successful EUR 3.9 billion project financing

cases.confidence_note: Timing: TAP AG, owned by foreign companies, ran the land programme with its consultant, and its shareholders paid costs before financing closed. The EIB and EBRD were still considering loans in 2016 and closed in December 2018, so their money came after the 2016 deals and financed the project those deals served. Farmer accounts come from Bankwatch interviews, and the report could not verify the date of one offer. TAP says expropriation pays the same as a negotiated deal; Bankwatch disputes this.

lvwhy.project: Foreign owners built the pipeline; banks later financed it.
lvwhy.land: Farm land and trees were taken for the corridor.

cases.title: Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan Pipeline in Turkey: Ardahan Villages and Ferhat Kaya
cases.point: Ardahan, the town where Ferhat Kaya was detained, and centre of the villages visited (approximate)

lenders.name: IFC
lenders.role: Approved funding in November 2003 (fact-finding report, 2005).

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
lenders.role: Approved funding in November 2003 (fact-finding report, 2005).

lenders.name: Export credit agencies
lenders.role: From the UK, US, Germany, Japan, Italy and France guaranteed credit (fact-finding report, 2005).

lenders.name: Commercial banks
lenders.role: 15 private banks, including ABN Amro, RBS and Citigroup; the project was 70% debt-financed (fact-finding report, 2005).

cases.conditions: Loan agreements set land acquisition standards. The UK government told Parliament there were significant breaches of project standards but that these did not justify suspending the loan (KHRP, 2005).

companies.name: BOTAŞ
companies.role: Turkish state company that built the Turkish section

cases.community: Land in the permanent corridor paid on average about 1.2 lira ($0.8) a square metre, against $1.5 in Azerbaijan and $3 in Georgia, and prices could not be bargained. A man in Otaglı lost 16,800 square metres and got nothing because the land was recorded as state land. Hasköy's 2,200 lira for common pasture went to the Treasury. Villagers reported damage in every village visited: waterlogged land at Çobanlı, an unrepaired 8 km road and milk yields down 50% at Hasköy, and cattle dying in trenches or from welding waste at Otaglı. In a breeding scheme run by a contractor of the project's community programme, examinations in most villages found only 5 to 15% of inseminated cows successful, with villagers estimating losses of about $100,000 at Çobanlı (fact-finding mission, 2005).
cases.suppression: Ferhat Kaya, DEHAP party chairman in Ardahan's central district, who helped villagers claim compensation, was detained on 5 May 2004. Witnesses saw blood on his clothes and deep cuts on his arms, and a medical report was described as consistent with ill-treatment (Bretton Woods Project; KHRP). Eleven police officers were later acquitted for lack of evidence; observers raised grave concerns about the fairness of the trial (KHRP). In March 2003, before the lenders' approval, gendarmes detained a fact-finding team near Ardahan twice in one day (OMCT). In 2005 gendarmes followed a mission, detained its drivers each night and questioned villagers after visits (fact-finding report).
cases.outcome: Many villagers were still waiting for compensation in 2005, and lenders did not suspend the loans. The police officers were acquitted.

sources.title: Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan Oil Pipeline: Fifth Fact Finding Mission, Ardahan
sources.publisher: Kurdish Human Rights Project, Corner House, Platform, Urgewald and others

sources.title: Baku-Ceyhan human rights activist arrested

Turkey: increased violence along a pipeline's route

cases.confidence_note: Most village losses are villagers' estimates recorded by campaign groups; the mission found crop payments were widely misunderstood as covering one year rather than three. A Turkish court acquitted the officers accused in the Kaya case. BTC Co and the lenders praised the project as a model of high standards. Lenders approved money in November 2003; BP's consortium was present throughout, and the 2004 and 2005 events came after approval.

lvwhy.land: Villagers' farm and pasture land was taken at fixed prices.

cases.title: Sakhalin II: Aniva Bay Dredging, Fishers and Indigenous Blockades
cases.place: Prigorodnoye LNG plant, Aniva Bay, Sakhalin, Russia
cases.point: LNG plant and jetty on Aniva Bay (approximate)

lenders.name: Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC)
lenders.role: Its predecessor financed Phase 1. JBIC and private banks signed the Phase 2 loan in June 2008, given as US$5.3 billion (FoE Japan), after the harm below.

cases.conditions: Phase 2 loan talks ran from 2001 while construction went on (Bankwatch). The EBRD called the environmental review "unfit for purpose" in June 2005 (Pacific Environment) and confirmed in January 2007 that it would not provide US$300 million (Swarthmore). US EXIM and the UK's ECGD stopped considering loans in March 2008 (FoE Japan).

companies.name: Sakhalin Energy (Shell 55%, Mitsui 25%, Mitsubishi 20%)
companies.role: Owner and builder when the dredging and spill happened; Gazprom took a majority in December 2006 (FoE Japan)

cases.community: About 2 million cubic metres of dredged waste were dumped in Aniva Bay (Bankwatch), which provides habitat for 25% of the salmon caught on Sakhalin (Pacific Environment, 2005). In August 2004 Sakhalin Energy banned salmon fishing near the plant site, and fishers blocked the plant road with cars loaded with nets (Platform). Photos taken about a year after dumping were described as showing "almost underwater desert" (Bankwatch). In September 2004 a contracted dredging ship ran aground near Kholmsk and spilled about 1,300 barrels of fuel oil along 5 km of coast; residents fell ill and cleanup began after 18 hours (Platform). Nivkh, Uilta, Evenk and Nanai groups said oil projects destroyed reindeer pasture and forests and depleted fish stocks (Swarthmore).
cases.suppression: Company representatives reportedly threatened to fire about 30 indigenous employees if they joined the protests (Swarthmore Global Nonviolent Action Database).
cases.outcome: Indigenous groups blockaded project roads in January and June 2005, and over 300 people blockaded the LNG plant on 28 January 2006. A Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk court rejected the review for the jetty and an appeal upheld it in 2005. A complaint to the EBRD's office, case 2005/01, was received on 26 July 2005 and closed in January 2007 as resolved outside the mechanism. A federal inspection agency recorded 97 violations in 155 visits (Platform). Campaigners did not win a cultural assessment.

sources.title: Sakhalin II Oil and Gas Project
Sakhalin II impacts
Pacific Environment press release on Aniva Bay court ruling
Indigenous peoples of Sakhalin campaign against oil extraction, 2005-2007
sources.publisher: Global Nonviolent Action Database, Swarthmore College

sources.title: LNG presentation on Sakhalin II
Sakhalin 2, complaint 2005/01
Independent Recourse Mechanism registry

cases.confidence_note: The tie at the time of the harm is foreign ownership: Shell, Mitsui and Mitsubishi owned the builder until December 2006. JBIC's Phase 2 money came in 2008, after the dredging and spill, and the EBRD did not fund Phase 2, so neither lender's money paid for these works. Sakhalin Energy said its dump zone should not cause sediment problems. No figures for fishers' lost catch were found. FoE Japan gives the spill as 200 tons. FoE Japan's page shows the Phase 2 amount both in US dollars and in yen.
cases.ecosystem: About 2 million cubic metres of dredge waste went into Aniva Bay, and the Kholmsk spill oiled 5 km of coast.

lvwhy.project: The foreign-owned builder's LNG jetty needed the dredging.
lvwhy.finance: JBIC and private banks later financed Phase 2.

cases.title: Tayan Nuur Iron Ore Mine: Gobi Altai Herders
cases.point: Tseel soum, where the Tayan Nuur mine operates (approximate)

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
lenders.role: Approved up to USD 30 million debt and up to USD 25 million equity in January 2012, as Category B (Bankwatch and SOMO, 2014).

cases.conditions: Action plans agreed with the bank; SOMO reports EBRD received no environmental or social information from the company after mid-2013.
cases.community: The company says 22 herder families were resettled between 2007 and 2011 with cash; no new land was allocated, and several families tried to go back to winter camps they had sold. Herders reported losing up to several dozen animals, mostly goats and camels, to dust illness, and one resettled herder said her herd had halved. The soum governor said well levels fell 3 to 4 metres since mining began; the bagh governor said Bayangol bagh lacked water for livestock for the first time in spring 2014. Ore trucks passed about every 15 minutes on a 168 km route to the border. The report contains no measured dust figures (Bankwatch and SOMO, 2014).
cases.suppression: The company filed up to seven defamation lawsuits against critics, including bagh governors and health workers, on charges carrying up to 22 years in prison. All were acquitted in May 2014. Herders said security staff intimidated them and kept them off the site; the Council of Natives reported cameras and phones taken and not returned (Bankwatch and SOMO, 2014).
cases.outcome: Seven people complained to the EBRD in December 2014. The office declined to host a dialogue but opened a compliance review, which recorded non-compliance; the case closed in May 2018 (SOMO; Accountability Console).

cases.conditions: Project cost about $650 million (IFC). IFC classed it Category A, its highest risk rating, and projected 14 families physically displaced and about 154 economically displaced (IFC).

companies.name: Nepal Water and Energy Development Company
companies.role: Developer, owned by Korea South-East Power (KOSEP, 50%), Daelim (15%), Kyeryong (10%), IFC (15%) and a local partner (IFC)

cases.community: About 40 households, about 240 people, lost private or Guthi land in 2013 and 2014, about 15 houses were affected, and about 76.7 hectares of community forest were taken (LAHURNIP, 2017). A Gumchet resident said road blasting ran 4 to 5 times a day for about nine months; another said stones punctured his roof, ruined crops, and the river carried off nine ropanis of land, and Gumchet's 16 households were paid NPR 5,000 each. The study found no free, prior and informed consent from the Tamang. Eight Dalit households cremate their dead on the riverbank, and no compensating measure was proposed. In 2023 Nepali Times reported that 110 households at Hakubesi and Phulbari were displaced with partial pay, and that one man's house lost a room after the river was diverted.
cases.killed_note: None counted. At least 60 people died in Haku wards 8 and 9 in landslides set off by the April 2015 earthquake; residents believe blasting weakened the slopes, the project rejects this, and it did not do the assessments communities asked for (LAHURNIP). Hundreds were reported trapped in hydropower tunnels in the August 2026 flood, with no death toll for this project (SANDRP).
cases.displaced_note: Nepali Times (2023): 110 households at Hakubesi and Phulbari displaced. LAHURNIP (2017): about 40 households lost land, about 15 houses affected. IFC projected 14 families physically and about 154 economically displaced.
cases.outcome: A consent agreement covers 10 of 21 project areas, activists said in 2023, with about Rs140 million for development over five years; community representatives said none had been released, while the developer blamed procedures with overseas partners. The project was heavily damaged by the 26 August 2026 flood and work stopped (SANDRP).

companies.role: British company registered in Guernsey, farm owner

cases.community: The farm's resettlement plan counted 230 households (about 1,258 people) directly affected: 80 lost homes and land, and 150 lost farmland. Villagers say they were offered TZS 10,000 (about $6) an acre, while the plan cited TZS 30,000 (about $17). In 2010 more than 600 farmers wrote to the company about crop loss and illness after aerial spraying; a Tanzanian pesticide institute hired by the company found glyphosate drift had damaged nearby farms, and 518 farmers had been paid by December 2011. Villagers say some others were not paid and allege that wells were contaminated. One microfinance lender reported about 50% default in 2013 among outgrowers, and villagers reported selling livestock and some homes and having goods seized. Rents rose from TZS 20,000-30,000 to about TZS 100,000 an acre (Oakland Institute, 2015).
cases.displaced_note: The farm's own resettlement plan counts 230 households, about 1,258 people, directly affected; 80 households lost homes (Oakland Institute, 2015).
cases.outcome: The company stopped production loans in 2014/15 and paid a yearly community fund of about TZS 50 million. Agrica shut down in 2019; a Tanzanian bank took over managing the farm and held an auction in October 2020 (farmlandgrab).

cases.title: Thwake Dam: Unpaid Land and Blasting Damage
cases.point: Mavindini ward, by the Thwake-Athi river confluence (approximate; exact position not confirmed)

lenders.name: African Development Bank
lenders.role: First financed the dam in 2013 with a $96.22 million African Development Fund package (Smart Water Magazine, 2026), added loans in November 2018 (Early Warning System), and approved €68.39 million more by mid-2026. A September 2026 review mission stressed timely payment to residents hit by blasting (Devdiscourse, 2026).

cases.conditions: Bank finance for a dam costing about Sh62.3 billion on the Athi River, with a compensation budget raised from Sh2.4 billion to Sh3.9 billion (Daily Nation).
cases.community: More than 500 families in Kitui and Makueni were supposed to leave by a February deadline, though many had no payment or only part; some payments left out houses, fruit trees and irrigation (Daily Nation). A petition by residents said some farmers were underpaid and people with no land in the area were paid, and several agencies investigated. In 2022 at least seven families at Katithi were living as squatters on taken land: paid for structures and trees but not land, waiting on succession steps, told not to farm because of machinery, and reporting children sick from dust (The Star). In August 2026 residents from 40 villages in Mavindini reported dust, noise and vibration and alleged house damage from blasting, and said homes near blasting sites were left out of damage assessments (Citizen Digital).
cases.outcome: Residents wrote to the bank in 2026 asking it to review their complaints and warned of pickets (Citizen Digital). The target for starting to fill the reservoir is January 2027.
